246.title: Judaism: hear
246.hook: the central declaration: hear, O Israel, the Lord is one (Deuteronomy 6:4)
246.howItsDone: Observant Jews recite the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, often covering their eyes; its words are written in the mezuzah on the doorpost and in tefillin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vesak, lanterns and a full moon to close the Buddhist visit. Your line was the full moon. Day two hundred forty-six, and a new visit: Judaism.

Six Hebrew words. Observant Jews say them twice a day, morning and night, often with a hand over the eyes. They're whispered to children at bedtime. They're written on a tiny scroll inside a case on the doorframe of Jewish homes. And Jewish tradition hopes they will be among a person's last words. The striking part is the very first word. It isn't believe, or pray, or obey. It's listen. Today's word: Shema.
screen: `SIX HEBREW WORDS, TWICE A DAY.` → `ON THE DOORFRAME, AT BEDTIME.` → `SHEMA.`

segments.voice: The words come from Deuteronomy, chapter six, verse four, where Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, it begins Shema Yisrael. Shema means hear, but it's a rich word: listen, pay attention, understand, take it to heart, even obey. It's hearing that changes what you do. And notice who's addressed: not one person alone, but Israel, the whole people. Then the next verse: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The passage goes on: these words should be on your heart, taught to your children, spoken when you sit at home and walk on the road, when you lie down and when you rise up, bound on your hand and written on your doorposts. Observant Jews do exactly that. The Shema is said in the morning and evening prayers. It's written inside the mezuzah on the doorpost and inside tefillin, the small leather boxes some Jews bind on the arm and head for weekday morning prayer. The custom is to cover the eyes while saying it, shutting out everything else to listen. A guest's note: when Jews read the divine name, written in English as LORD, they don't pronounce it, but say Adonai, my Lord, instead. The Talmud tells of Rabbi Akiva, put to death by the Romans, dying with the Shema's last word, one, on his lips. The center of Jewish faith begins with an open ear.

segments.voice: If you like, cover your eyes with your hand, as is the custom for the Shema, and just hear: the nearest sound, then something farther away, the hum of the room, your own breath. Don't name them or judge them; let hearing be the whole practice.
Shema. Hebrew for hear, listen, take to heart: the first word of Judaism's central declaration, said morning and night. Today's word.
Your line: hear. Fully, to take it to heart, not just waiting for your turn. Day two hundred forty-six, done.

247.title: Judaism: covenant
247.hook: a people bound to God through Abraham, Sinai and the Torah
247.howItsDone: Jews understand their life of Torah and commandments as living within the covenant; brit milah, circumcision on the eighth day, marks a baby boy's entry into the covenant of Abraham, and many communities hold a naming ceremony for girls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema, six words that begin with listen. Your line was hear. Day two hundred forty-seven.

Think of the difference between a contract and a marriage. A contract says: if you do this, I'll do that, and if you don't, we're done. A marriage says something stranger: we belong to each other now, through good years and bad, and even when one of us fails, the bond is still there to come back to. Jews have a word for the relationship between God and the Jewish people, much closer to the second than the first. It runs through the whole Hebrew Bible. Today's word: brit.
screen: `A CONTRACT, OR A MARRIAGE?` → `A BOND TO COME BACK TO.` → `BRIT.`

segments.voice: Brit is Hebrew for covenant, a binding promise between two parties. The Torah tells of several. After the flood, God makes a covenant with Noah and every living thing, never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets a rainbow in the clouds as its sign. Jewish tradition sees that covenant as embracing all humanity. Then Abraham. God promises him descendants as many as the stars and a land for them, and the sign is circumcision, brit milah, still performed for Jewish baby boys on the eighth day, which is why many people know the word as bris. Then Sinai, the great one. The people, freed from Egypt, stand at the foot of the mountain. Moses reads them the book of the covenant, and in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation they answer: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, naaseh venishma: literally, we will do, and we will hear. The rabbis of the Talmud loved that order: doing before fully understanding, like people in love who say yes before they know every detail. At Sinai the covenant is the Torah itself, the teaching and the commandments, a whole way of life given and received. And Deuteronomy says it was made not only with those standing there that day, but with those not yet there. Many Jews understand that to include every Jewish generation since. The covenant runs two ways: God bound to a people, and a people bound to God. Jews have argued with it, struggled with it and wept over it for thousands of years. They've also kept it.

248.title: Judaism: study is holy
248.hook: learning is itself worship, and argument is honored (Pirkei Avot 1.1)
248.howItsDone: Many Jews study Torah and Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating line by line, and a weekly portion of the Torah is read in synagogue through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brit, the covenant: a people bound to God by a promise. Your line was a promise kept. Day two hundred forty-eight.

A room full of long tables. Two people sit across from each other with one big book open between them, and they are arguing. Not whispering. Arguing, out loud, fingers on the page, one shaking her head, the other laughing. Pair after pair like that, all at once, loud as a train station. To a stranger it might sound like something has gone wrong. In a traditional Jewish house of study, it's the sound of something going right. Today: why study itself can be holy, and why the arguing is part of it.
screen: `A ROOM OF LONG TABLES.` → `PAIRS, ARGUING OUT LOUD.` → `THE SOUND OF SOMETHING GOING RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Torah. In the narrowest sense it means the five books of Moses, the scroll in the ark of a synagogue. The Hebrew root has to do with teaching, pointing the way, so the word also stretches to mean all Jewish teaching, the whole conversation that grew around the scroll. That conversation has a famous first line. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, a short book of sayings in the Mishnah, opens by tracing a chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and on to the teachers of the great assembly. Learning is handed from person to person, like a lamp passed down a line. The Torah itself asks for this. Right after the Shema, Deuteronomy says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." Teaching the young isn't a hobby here; it sits inside the central prayer. Then the surprise: Jewish tradition honors argument. The Talmud records the debates of two ancient schools, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, who disagreed again and again. A heavenly voice, the story goes, declared that both were the words of the living God, and the law followed Hillel partly because his students were humble and taught Shammai's view before their own. And study often happens in pairs, called chavruta, from the word for friend. You don't learn alone. You push, your partner pushes back, and the text opens.

249.title: Judaism: repair
249.hook: many Jews speak of repairing the world, a phrase with old mystical and modern meanings
249.howItsDone: Many Jewish communities and families organize acts of service, charity and advocacy under the name tikkun olam; some also connect everyday commandments and blessings to Isaac Luria's idea of lifting sparks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Torah, teaching handed hand to hand and argued over in pairs. Your line was learn together. Day two hundred forty-nine.

Somewhere in your home there's a thing that's been broken for months. A drawer that sticks. A lamp with a loose switch. A shirt missing one button, folded at the bottom of the pile. You walk past it every day. It's too small to matter, and somehow too annoying to fix. Now zoom out. The street has its broken things too. So does the town, the country, the whole world, and all of it can feel far too big for one person. Jewish tradition has a phrase that sits right between the button and the world. Today: tikkun olam.
screen: `THE DRAWER THAT STICKS.` → `THE WORLD THAT FEELS TOO BIG.` → `TIKKUN OLAM.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repair, or setting right. Olam means world. Repairing the world. Today many Jews use the phrase for acts of justice and kindness: feeding people, protecting the vulnerable, caring for the earth. But the phrase has lived several lives. The first life is legal. In the Mishnah, the rabbis made certain adjustments to the law, about divorce documents and freeing captives, and gave their reason as for the repair of the world, meaning to keep society in good working order. The second life is in prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of Jewish services, hopes for a day when the world will be set right under the kingship of God. The third life is mystical. In the sixteenth century, in the hill town of Safed, the teacher Isaac Luria told a remarkable story. At creation, divine light was poured into vessels too fragile to hold it, and they shattered. Sparks of holiness fell and scattered into everything. Every good deed, every blessing, every commandment kept, lifts a spark back up and helps mend what broke. In modern times the phrase grew wider again, and many Jewish groups made it a banner for social action. Jews themselves debate how the old and new meanings fit together, and that debate is part of the story. And Pirkei Avot keeps a saying from Rabbi Tarfon: it isn't your job to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either.
screen: `TIKKUN — REPAIR. OLAM — WORLD.` · `FOR THE GOOD ORDER OF THE WORLD.` · `SHATTERED VESSELS, SCATTERED SPARKS.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT YOURS TO QUIT.` · then, large: `REPAIR.`

segments.voice: Let one broken thing come to mind: the sticking drawer, the loose button, a message you owe someone, a small promise that cracked. Choose one you could mend, and picture your hands doing it, start to finish. Not the world, just one spark.
Tikkun olam. Repairing the world: a legal phrase, a line of prayer, a mystical picture of gathering sparks, and a call to justice. Today's word.
Your line: repair. One spark lifted is one small corner of the world mended. See you tomorrow.

250.title: Judaism: blessings
250.hook: a blessing for bread, for thunder, for a rainbow: noticing through words
250.howItsDone: Observant Jews say a bracha before and after eating and at many moments of the day, from waking to seeing lightning or a rainbow, and many aim for a hundred blessings daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tikkun olam, repairing the world one spark at a time. Your line was repair. Day two hundred fifty.

Thunder rolls over the house. The usual response: a flinch, a look out the window, maybe the weather app. Now suppose the first response, before any of that, was a sentence. A short, fixed sentence learned for exactly this moment. Another for the first rainbow after the storm. Another for the first bite of bread. Another for new shoes, or seeing the ocean after a long time away. Your whole day would be stitched with small sentences, each one a way of noticing. In Jewish life, there really is a sentence for all of these. Today: the bracha, the blessing.
screen: `THUNDER OVER THE HOUSE.` → `A SENTENCE FOR THIS MOMENT.` → `THE BRACHA.`

segments.voice: Bracha, blessing. A standard blessing opens with fixed words: baruch atah Adonai, eloheinu melech ha-olam. Blessed are you, Lord our God, ruler of the universe. Then comes the ending that fits the moment. Before bread: who brings forth bread from the earth. That's the blessing called hamotzi. For thunder: whose strength and might fill the world. For a rainbow: who remembers the covenant and keeps the promise, a nod back to Noah, and to brit, the covenant, from a few days ago. Why bless before eating something you already have? The Talmud gives a sharp answer. It quotes a psalm, in the King James words, "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof," and reasons that enjoying anything from the world without a blessing is like taking what isn't yours. The blessing is a kind of asking permission and a kind of thank-you, at once. There's even a goal. The Talmud records a teaching of Rabbi Meir that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. The daily prayers, the meals and the moments are how an observant day can add up to it. A blessing makes you stop and name the thing. You can't bless bread you haven't noticed. You can't bless thunder while scrolling past it. The fixed words do the noticing for you, until noticing becomes a habit.
screen: `BLESSED ARE YOU, RULER OF THE UNIVERSE.` · `BREAD, THUNDER, RAINBOW.` · `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS A DAY.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS.`

segments.voice: Pick something plain, a cup of water, the chair holding you, the light through the window, and look at it properly, as if it were new. If you pray, you can say the traditional opening, blessed are you; if you don't, simply name it slowly: this water, this chair, this light. Let the naming be the thank-you.
Bracha. A blessing: a fixed sentence that begins blessed are you, and turns bread, thunder and rainbows into moments noticed. Today's word.
Your line: blessed is. Two words, and the ordinary gets noticed. Two hundred fifty days now.

251.title: Judaism: Shabbat candles
251.hook: on Friday at dusk, two candles are lit and rest begins
251.howItsDone: In many Jewish homes, two candles are lit shortly before sunset on Friday with a blessing, the eyes covered, and Shabbat is kept until nightfall on Saturday; how strictly varies from family to family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bracha, the blessing, a sentence for bread and thunder. Your line was blessed is.

Friday, late afternoon. The inbox still open, the groceries half put away, the phone buzzing with plans. At the same hour, in a Jewish home, a kitchen table is set. Someone strikes a match and lights two candles. She draws her hands around the flames three times, covers her eyes, and says a blessing. When she uncovers them, nothing in the room has moved, and yet the week is over. Until nightfall tomorrow, it's Shabbat.
screen: `FRIDAY, THE INBOX STILL OPEN.` → `A MATCH, TWO FLAMES.` → `THE WEEK IS OVER.`

segments.voice: Shabbat means rest, or ceasing. It runs from just before sunset on Friday until nightfall on Saturday. Why two candles? A common answer: the Ten Commandments appear twice in the Torah. In Exodus the commandment begins, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society words, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy it begins with a different verb: observe it, or guard it. Remember, and keep. One candle for each. In many homes the woman of the house lights them, though anyone may, and a little before sunset, so no one lights a fire once Shabbat has begun. That's why the eyes are covered. A blessing usually comes before the act, but here the blessing is what begins the rest, so you light, hide the flames, bless, and then look. The big idea: for six days, the Torah says, God made the world, and on the seventh God rested. Shabbat invites people to copy that rhythm. No work, no buying and selling, in many homes no phones or driving. Observance varies widely: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews keep it in very different ways. The twentieth-century teacher Abraham Joshua Heschel called Shabbat a palace in time: most holy places are buildings, but this one is built out of hours. And an old saying from the writer Ahad Ha'am turns it around: more than the Jews have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jews.

Your line: rest arrives. You don't have to chase it; at sundown, it comes. That's day two hundred fifty-one.

252.title: Passover, the freedom meal
252.hook: each year families retell the going out from Egypt around a table (Exodus 12)
252.howItsDone: Each spring Jewish families hold a Seder on the first night of Passover (the first two nights in many communities outside Israel), reading the Haggadah, eating matzah and bitter herbs, and answering the children's questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabbat, two candles for remember and keep. Your line was rest arrives. Today, the last day of our visit to Judaism.

A long table, extra chairs borrowed from the neighbors. A plate in the middle with odd things on it: a bone, a roasted egg, bitter herbs, a paste of apples and nuts. Crackers that look like they've been ironed flat. The youngest child at the table stands up, a little nervous, and asks the question everyone has been waiting for: why is this night different from all other nights? The grown-ups answer with an ancient story, told as if it happened to them. Today: Pesach, Passover.
screen: `A PLATE OF ODD THINGS.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `PESACH.`

segments.voice: Exodus tells the story. The Israelites are slaves in Egypt. Moses asks Pharaoh to let them go, plagues fall, and on the last night God passes over the houses of the Israelites, marked with the blood of a lamb. Pesach comes from that verb: to pass over. They leave in such a hurry the bread has no time to rise, which is why the flat bread, matzah, is eaten for the whole festival. Then the Torah does something unusual: it commands the retelling. In the King James words: "And thou shalt shew thy son in that day, saying, This is done because of that which the LORD did unto me when I came forth out of Egypt." Unto me, not unto my ancestors. The Mishnah takes that seriously: in every generation, a person should see themselves as if they personally went out of Egypt. So the Seder, the ordered meal, is built to make you taste it. Bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery. Salt water for tears. Four cups of wine for freedom. The book at the table, the Haggadah, answers the child's question with today's line: we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and now we are free. Look back at the week. Shema, hear. Brit, a promise kept. Torah, learned together. Tikkun olam, repair. Bracha, blessed is. Shabbat, rest arrives. And Pesach: a people who remember freedom by eating it, together, every year.
screen: `PESACH — TO PASS OVER.` · `NO TIME FOR THE BREAD TO RISE.` · `AS IF YOU WENT OUT YOURSELF.` · `BITTER HERBS, SALT WATER, FOUR CUPS.` · then, large: `WE WERE SLAVES, NOW FREE.`

segments.voice: Remember one story of freedom: a family story of someone who crossed a border, left a bad job, got sober, walked out of something, or your own. Tell it to yourself the Passover way, as if it happened to you, in the present tense. Notice what was bitter, and what was sweet.
Pesach. Passover: the festival that retells the going out from Egypt around a table, so each generation tastes freedom. Today's word.
Your line: we were slaves, now free. Tomorrow, a new visit: Christianity. Day two hundred fifty-two, done.
